meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Why Don't You Carry a Wrist Watch Like Everyone Else?'?
meta.ogDescription: A Punch cartoon gag from 1907, not a Beerbohm Tree quip. Yogi Berra denied his version of it outright.

answer.label: Not Herbert Beerbohm Tree — a Punch joke that predates him
answer.sourceLine: Nobody owns this line. The oldest version anyone has found is a Punch cartoon of March 1907, drawn by the magazine’s F. H. Townsend, in which a passer-by asks a man burdened with a clock whether he would not find it more convenient to carry a watch. For the next forty years the joke was retold with the speaker variously an Irishman’s heckler, a drunk, a boy on roller skates and a knocked-over woman — which is the wording quoted here. Tree acquired it in 1956; Yogi Berra acquired it in 1960 and publicly disowned it.

source.excerpt: Funny Man. “Pardon me, Sir, but wouldn’t you find it more convenient to carry a watch?”
trail: The chronology here is Quote Investigator’s ↗, which dates the earliest instance to a Punch cartoon of March 1907 by F. H. Townsend and tracks the retellings through 1911, 1912, 1913, 1921, 1928, 1940, 1945, 1946, 1956 and 1960.

Tree’s version is the one printed in Hesketh Pearson’s 1956 biography and it is not this sentence: Wikiquote’s Tree page ↗ carries it as “My poor fellow, why not carry a watch?”, said “to a man who was staggering in the street under the weight of a grandfather clock”.

The attribution to Yogi Berra is refuted by Berra himself. Quote Investigator quotes his 1961 autobiography on a televised version: “I never said that, either. If I could think of funny things like that, I would be working for Bob Hope.”

We tried to reach the cartoon itself in the Internet Archive’s scan of Punch, January–June 1907 ↗ and could not: the phrase does not appear in that volume’s OCR, so the 1907 caption rests on Quote Investigator’s reproduction alone.
source.excerptNote: That is the 1907 caption as reproduced by Quote Investigator; we could not confirm it independently, because the Internet Archive’s scan of Punch volume 132 does not yield the caption in its OCR. The wrist-watch wording quoted on this page is closest to a 1945 Reader’s Digest version, which reads “everybody else” rather than “everyone else”.

author.name: Unknown (a 1907 Punch cartoon joke)
author.heading: About the source of this joke
author.metaLine: Earliest known appearance: Punch, March 1907 · author unrecorded
author.bio: No author is known. The joke’s oldest documented appearance is an unsigned cartoon caption in Punch in March 1907, drawn by the magazine’s illustrator F. H. Townsend; Punch captions of the period were often worked up editorially rather than credited to a writer. It was reprinted in American newspapers within months and retold for the next four decades with a different speaker almost every time, which is why the wording quoted today matches none of the early versions exactly.

copyAttribution: This is a floating joke, not a quotation. Its earliest known appearance is a Punch cartoon of March 1907 drawn by F. H. Townsend — “Pardon me, Sir, but wouldn't you find it more convenient to carry a watch?” The wrist-watch wording belongs to later retellings, and the line was credited to Herbert Beerbohm Tree only in 1956, in different words.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A joke with no author collects famous ones. Four names have been attached to this one in print, and the earliest instance carries none of them.

items.why: Hesketh Pearson’s 1956 biography gives Tree the remark “My poor fellow, why not carry a watch?” — published 39 years after Tree’s death in 1917, and half a century after the Punch cartoon ↗. It is also not the wrist-watch wording quoted here.
Joe Garagiola’s 1960 book put Berra on the receiving end of the line; a televised retelling then had Berra deliver it. In his 1961 autobiography Berra answered: “I never said that, either.”

In 1913 and again in 1914 the joke was credited to du Maurier, who had died in 1896, and it was even voted the “world’s best joke” on that basis. The 1907 cartoon was drawn by F. H. Townsend ↗. Quote Investigator allows that an earlier du Maurier cartoon may exist but reports it has not located one.

The heckler is an inebriate in 1911, a drunken man in 1912, a boy on roller skates in 1913, a “pre-Volstead man” in 1921 and a knocked-down woman in 1945. The instability of the scene is the clearest sign this is a gag in circulation rather than a remembered remark.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no original speaker to name. The oldest known version is a cartoon caption printed in Punch in March 1907, and every famous name attached to the joke since then arrived decades later — as Quote Investigator documents ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a small machine for showing how attribution actually works. It began anonymous, in a magazine that printed gags by the hundred, and then drifted toward whoever was famous for being funny at the time — a celebrated Edwardian actor-manager in Britain, a celebrated malapropist ballplayer in America.

What makes it unusually well documented is that one of those men objected. Berra spent a career having lines invented for him, and his autobiography is unusual in the quotation record for flatly denying a joke that flattered him.
detailsBody: Punch was the dominant British humour magazine of the period, and F. H. Townsend (1868–1920) was a staff illustrator who became its first art editor. A caption like this one was house work, not authored wit, which is part of why no name travelled with the joke.

Tree (1852–1917) was an actor-manager famous enough for his own anthology of quips, and such collections are where orphan jokes tend to land. The 1956 biography that first gives him this one is sympathetic rather than source-critical, and it supplies no date, place or witness.
context.pull: It began as nobody's line. Fame supplied the rest.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator dates the earliest instance of the joke to a March 1907 Punch cartoon by Frederick Henry Townsend captioned “Pardon me, Sir, but wouldn't you find it more convenient to carry a watch?”, records the 1956 Hesketh Pearson biography crediting Tree with “My poor fellow, why not carry a watch?”, the 1945 Reader's Digest wording, and Berra's 1961 denial.
Wikiquote's Herbert Beerbohm Tree page carries “My poor fellow, why not carry a watch?” with the grandfather-clock setting — not the wrist-watch wording.
Herbert Beerbohm Tree lived 17 December 1852 to 2 July 1917 and was an English actor-manager.
Frederick Henry Townsend (25 February 1868 - 11 December 1920) was a British illustrator, cartoonist and art editor of Punch.
The March 1907 Punch cartoon caption could NOT be located in the OCR of the Internet Archive scan of Punch volume 132 (January-June 1907), so the caption rests on Quote Investigator alone.
